question: How many identical layers make up the encoder stack of the Transformer in 'Attention Is All You Need', and what is the model dimension d_model?
expected_answer: The encoder is a stack of N = 6 identical layers; all sub-layers and embedding layers produce outputs of dimension d_model = 512.
notes: Evidence: 'The encoder is composed of a stack of N = 6 identical layers.' and 'produce outputs of dimension dmodel = 512' (p. 3)

question: How many total parameters do BERT-Base and BERT-Large have?
expected_answer: BERT-Base has 110M parameters (L=12, H=768, A=12) and BERT-Large has 340M parameters (L=24, H=1024, A=16).
notes: Evidence: 'BERTBASE (L=12, H=768, A=12, Total Parameters=110M) and BERTLARGE (L=24, H=1024, A=16, Total Parameters=340M)' (p. 3); restated 'BERT BASE contains 110M parameters and BERT LARGE contains 340M parameters' (p. 8)

question: What knowledge source does the RAG model use for its non-parametric memory, and how many documents does the index contain?
expected_answer: A December 2018 Wikipedia dump, with each article split into disjoint 100-word chunks, giving 21M documents indexed with FAISS (MIPS index).
notes: Evidence: 'we use the December 2018 dump. Each Wikipedia article is split into disjoint 100-word chunks, to make a total of 21M documents.' (p. 4)

question: According to the Sentence-BERT paper, how long does finding the most similar pair in a collection of 10,000 sentences take with BERT compared to SBERT?
expected_answer: About 65 hours with BERT (about 50 million inference computations) versus about 5 seconds with SBERT.
notes: Evidence: 'This reduces the effort for finding the most similar pair from 65 hours with BERT / RoBERTa to about 5 seconds with SBERT' (p. 1); also p. 2 ('~5 seconds with SBERT')

question: What BLEU scores did the big Transformer model achieve on WMT 2014 English-to-German and English-to-French, and how long and on what hardware was it trained?
expected_answer: 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German and 41.8 BLEU on English-to-French; training took 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs (300,000 steps).
notes: Evidence: 'Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German ... BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs' (p. 1); 'The big models were trained for 300,000 steps (3.5 days)' (p. 7); 'Training took 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs.' (p. 8). Facts are spread across abstract, training section and results section.

question: Describe BERT's two pre-training tasks, including how tokens are masked and how sentence pairs are constructed.
expected_answer: (1) Masked LM: 15% of token positions are chosen at random; a chosen token is replaced with [MASK] 80% of the time, a random token 10% of the time, and left unchanged 10% of the time, and the model predicts the original token. (2) Next Sentence Prediction: for sentence pairs A/B, 50% of the time B is the actual next sentence (IsNext) and 50% of the time a random sentence (NotNext).
notes: Evidence: 'chooses 15% of the token positions at random ... (1) the [MASK] token 80% of the time (2) a random token 10% of the time (3) the unchanged i-th token 10% of the time' and '50% of the time B is the actual next sentence that follows A (labeled as IsNext), and 50% of the time it is a random sentence' (p. 4); worked masking example in Appendix (p. 12)

question: What is the difference between the RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token models?
expected_answer: RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document to generate the complete output sequence (the document is a single latent variable marginalized over the top-k). RAG-Token can draw a different latent document for each target token and marginalizes per token, letting the generator choose content from several documents.
notes: Evidence: 'The RAG-Sequence model uses the same retrieved document to generate the complete sequence.' and 'In the RAG-Token model we can draw a different latent document for each target token and marginalize accordingly.' (p. 3); decoding differences in Sec. 2.5 (p. 4)

question: Why are raw BERT outputs a poor choice for sentence embeddings compared with cosine similarity, and how does Sentence-BERT address this?
expected_answer: Using BERT as a cross-encoder for similarity search is computationally infeasible (e.g. ~65 hours for 10,000 sentences), and the common shortcuts (averaging BERT output or the [CLS] token) give bad sentence embeddings, worse than averaged GloVe (avg. STS correlation 54.81 for averaged BERT and 29.19 for CLS). SBERT adds a pooling operation (default MEAN) and fine-tunes BERT/RoBERTa in siamese/triplet networks so the embeddings are semantically meaningful and comparable with cosine similarity.
notes: Evidence: 'this common practice yields rather bad sentence embeddings, often worse than averaging GloVe embeddings' (p. 1); 'The default configuration is MEAN. In order to fine-tune BERT / RoBERTa, we create siamese and triplet networks' (p. 3); 'Averaging the BERT embeddings achieves an average correlation of only 54.81, and using the CLS-token output only achieves an average correlation of 29.19.' (p. 4)

question: How does the RAG model build on BERT, and what component does it use for generation?
expected_answer: RAG's retriever (DPR) is a bi-encoder whose document encoder and query encoder are both based on BERT-Base (110M parameters each, the BERT-Base size reported in the BERT paper); the document encoder and index are kept fixed while the query encoder is fine-tuned. Generation uses BART-large, a pre-trained seq2seq transformer (~400M parameters).
notes: Evidence: 'd(z) is a dense representation of a document produced by a BERTBASE document encoder ... query encoder, also based on BERTBASE' and 'We use BART-large ... with 400M parameters' (p. 3, RAG); 'keep the document encoder (and index) fixed' (p. 4, RAG); 'BERT-base query and document encoder of DPR, with 110M parameters each' (p. 18, RAG); BERTBASE Total Parameters=110M (p. 3, BERT). Cross-document question.

question: Why does Sentence-BERT use the [CLS] token output as its default pooling strategy?
expected_answer: False premise: SBERT's default pooling strategy is MEAN (mean of all output vectors), not CLS; the paper also shows the raw BERT CLS vector gives poor sentence embeddings. The system should correct the premise.
notes: Evidence: 'Using the output of the CLS-token, computing the mean of all output vectors (MEAN-strategy), and computing a max-over-time of the output vectors (MAX-strategy). The default configuration is MEAN.' (p. 3)
